source.title: Grothendieck’s inequality and completely correlation preserving functions - a summary of recent results and an indication of related research problems

accepted.question_text: For the real and complex fields F in {R, C}, determine the exact numerical values of the Grothendieck constants K_G^R and K_G^C, where K_G^F is the least constant K for which every finite matrix (a_ij) over F and every choice of unit vectors u_i and v_j in an F-Hilbert space satisfy |Σ_i Σ_j a_ij ⟨u_i, v_j⟩| ≤ K sup{|Σ_i Σ_j a_ij p_i q_j| : |p_i| = |q_j| = 1}. If exact values cannot yet be obtained, develop methods that approximate K_G^R and K_G^C from above and below using the paper’s proposed framework of block matrix analysis, Gaussian random vectors, special functions, copulas, and combinatorics.

evidence.quote: The smallest possible value of the corresponding constant K is called the Grothendieck constant K F G. The superscripts R and C are used to indicate the different values in the real and complex case.

Computing the exact numerical value of the constants K R G and K C G is still an open problem (unsolved since 1953). Here, our own research activities are attached. We look for a general framework (primarily build on methods originating from (block) matrix analysis, multivariate statistics with real and complex Gaussian random vectors, theory of special functions, modelling of statistical dependence with copulas and combinatorics, whose complexity increases rapidly in dimension, though) which allows us either to give the value of K R G, respectively K C G explicitly or to approximate these values from above and from below at least.

Apart from its comprehensive mathematical fascination and richness the highly fascinating open problem of determining the value of the both Grothendieck constants K R G and K C G meanwhile is deeply linked with different fields, even including applications in computer science, high-dimensional data analyis and quantum mechanics.

accepted.question_text: For F in {R, C} and k ≥ 1, let C(k; F) be the set of k by k correlation matrices over F, let C1(k; F) be the subset of rank-one correlation matrices, and let acx denote absolute convex hull. Determine whether the trace-inequality form of Grothendieck’s inequality remains valid when the special block matrix J(A) = (1/2)[[0, A], [A*, 0]] is replaced by an arbitrary matrix B in M(k × k; F); equivalently, determine whether C(k; F) is contained in K_G^F acx(C1(k; F)) for every k.

evidence.quote: Of particular relevance is the set C1(k; F) of all k × k correlation matrices of rank 1 and the (Hermitian) block matrix J(A) := 1/2 ( 0 A A∗ 0 ), where m, n ∈ N and A ∈ M(m × n; F).

However, we don’t know whether we also may substitute in GT itself the block matrix J(A) through an arbitrary matrix B ∈ M(k × k; F). If this were the case an application of the bipolar theorem shows that the latter would be equivalent to the non-negligible set inclusion C(k; F) ⊆ K F G acx ( C1(k; F) ) for all k ∈ N, where C(k; F) denotes the set of all k × k correlation matrices with entries in F and acx the absolute convex hull (of a set).

accepted.question_text: Find functions b: R^k → {-1, 1}, with k ≥ 1, that are different from the sign function and whose associated completely correlation-preserving function h_b satisfies the workflow needed to improve the known upper bound for the real Grothendieck constant: h_b(0)=0, h_b is a homeomorphism, its inverse g_b=h_b^{-1} has an absolutely summable real Taylor expansion, the absolute-coefficient series f_b has f_b(r)=1 for some 0<r<1, and the resulting theorem gives K_G^R ≤ 1/r.
accepted.context_brief: Better CCP functions for K_G^R bounds

evidence.quote: All of these conditions are satisfied for the Grothendieck function and the Haagerup function and were used to construct a “small” upper bound of the respective Grothendieck constant. However, if we wish to apply these steps to a “better fitting function” b which is different from both, the Grothendieck function and the Haagerup function, we are strongly confronted with non-trivial persistent combinatorial issues; described in Section 5 below.
Assume that the assumptions (H) and (RA) of the workflow hold. Let fb : Dd −→ Fd be constructed as above and assume that fb satisfies the condition (PI(1)) for some 0 < r ∗ < 1. Then K F G ≤ 1/r∗.

So, if we wish to reduce the value of the upper bound of the real Grothendieck constant we have to look for functions b : Rk −→ {− 1, 1} which are different from sign : R −→ {− 1, 1}. However, these functions should satisfy all of the conditions in the listed workflow above.

accepted.question_text: Let h_b(ρ)=Σ_{n≥1} α_n ρ^n be the real one-dimensional completely correlation-preserving function attached to b, let g_b=h_b^{-1} have Taylor coefficients β_n, and let the proposed inverse-series pattern be nβ_n α_1^(2n−1) = −n α_1^(n−2) α_n + Σ_{k=2}^{n−2} (−1)^k m_k binom(n−1+k,k) α_1^((n−1)−k) p_k(α_2,…,α_n) + (−1)^(n−1) binom(2(n−1),n−1) α_2^(n−1), where p_k is indexed by a set A_k of integer multi-indices. For n ≥ 4 and 2 ≤ k ≤ n−2, prove this representation and determine the sets A_k and the numbers m_k explicitly, if this is feasible.

evidence.quote: It appears to us that there is a general pattern in these formulas which might lead to an expression of the following type: nβn α2n− 1 1 = − nαn− 2 1 αn+ n− 2∑ k=2 (− 1)k mk ((n − 1) + k k) α(n− 1)− k 1 pk(α2, α3, . . . , αn)+(− 1)n− 1 (2(n − 1) n − 1) αn− 1 2, where mk ∈ [k], pk(α2, α3, . . . , αn) := ∑(ν2,...,νn)∈ Ak ∏n l=2 ανl l and Ak ⊂ {µ ∈ Nn− 1 0 : ∑n l=2 l µl− 1 = n − 1 + k}.

(1-RP1) Let n ∈ N4 and k ∈ { 2, 3, . . . , n− 2}. Recall that nβn α2n− 1 1 = − nαn− 2 1 αn+ n− 2∑ k=2 (− 1)k mk ((n − 1) + k k) α(n− 1)− k 1 pk(α2, α3, . . . , αn)+(− 1)n− 1 (2(n − 1) n − 1) αn− 1 2. Prove this representation and determine Ak and the numbers mk therein explicitly (if feasible at all)!

accepted.question_text: Develop a structural theory of ordinary partial Bell polynomials sufficient for Taylor-series inversion problems arising from non-completely-correlation-preserving inverse functions, including closed-form or computationally effective descriptions of the Bell-polynomial values that enter the inverse coefficients β_n; methods may include high-performance computing, algebraic software, and induction principles stronger than ordinary induction when appropriate.

evidence.quote: The strong difficulties are twofold: already in the one-dimensional case we need to know the explicit value of all of the Fourier coefficients ⟨b, Hn⟩γ1, together with a closed form expression (if available at all) of all of the coefficients βn, where the latter involves (in general, unknown values of) ordinary partial Bell polynomials. It appears to us that in general one cannot use proofs by standard induction on n ∈ N to verify statements about Bell polynomials. Here, the Noetherian Induction Principle seems to be more appropriate.

Therefore, given the intrinsic combinatoric and computational complexity regarding the determination of the Taylor series coefficients of the Taylor series of the non-CCP function gb (via the Fa´ a-di Bruno formula), related research problems (which actually do not require any knowledge of the Grothendieck inequality) could be the following ones:
(1-RP2) Continue to investigate the structure of partial Bell polynomials; possibly with the aid of high-performance computers and related (algebraic) software tools.

accepted.question_text: Find a closed-form formula, or prove appropriate structural results, for the Taylor coefficients of the inverse of the complex Haagerup function z ↦ (π/4) z · ₂F₁(1/2, 1/2, 2; |z|²), whose inverse coefficients are needed for the complex-field version of the completely correlation-preserving-function approach to Grothendieck’s inequality.

evidence.quote: Unfortunately, a closed form representation of the coefficients of the inverse of a Taylor series runs against a well-known combinatorial complexity issue (due to the presence of ordinary partial Bell polynomials as building blocks of these coefficients - cf. research problem 7.1 below for details), which in general does not allow a closed form representation of these coefficients, such as is the case with the inverse of Haagerup’s function D ∋ z ↦→ π/4 z 2F1(1/2, 1/2, 2; |z|2) in the complex case.

An even stronger problem appears in the complex case, since already a closed-form formula for the coefficients of the Taylor series of the inverse of the Haagerup function is still unknown (cf. [ 17]).

accepted.question_text: For a Gaussian-copula parameter p with 0<p<1 and p≠1/2, determine whether there exists a function χ_p: R → {-1, 1} such that the Gaussian-copula correlation function ψ(p,p;ρ) equals h_{χ_p}(ρ)=E[χ_p(X)χ_p(Y)] for every ρ in [-1,1] when (X,Y) is a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance matrix Σ_2(ρ); equivalently, determine whether this ψ(p,p;·) can satisfy the workflow’s SIGN condition through some sign-valued function χ_p.

evidence.quote: If we thouroughly overhaul the CCP function [− 1, 1] ∋ ρ ↦→ 2/π arcsin(ρ) we recognise that some knowledge of Gaussian copulas (i.e., finite-dimensional multivariate distribution functions of univariate marginals generated by the distribution function of Gaussian random vectors) and (the probabilistic version) of the Hermite polynomials might become very fruitful regarding our indicated search for different “ suitable” CCP functions.

(2-RP1) Prove whether there are p ∈ (− 1, 1) \ { 1/2} and functions χp : R −→ {− 1, 1} such that ψ(p, p; ρ) = hχp(ρ) = E[χp(X) χp(Y)] for all ρ ∈ [− 1, 1] and (X, Y ) ∼ N2(0, Σ 2(ρ)), so that the condition (SIGN) of our workflow is satisfied for hχp.

accepted.question_text: Generalize the tetrachoric-series approach for the bivariate Gaussian copula to the n-variate Gaussian-copula setting for n ≥ 3, and formulate the corresponding version of the χ_p-realization problem: whether the resulting multivariate copula-based correlation functions arise from suitable sign-valued functions in the workflow for Grothendieck-type bounds.

evidence.quote: (2-RP2) Generalise the above approach (which is built on the tetrachoric series of the bivariate Gaussian copula) to the n-variate case, where n ∈ N3 and adapt problem (2-RP1) accordingly.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether the Gaussian-copula approach used to generalize Grothendieck’s identity in the real case can be transferred to the complex field, and whether such a transfer would yield an analogous generalization of Haagerup’s identity for complex Gaussian random vectors.

evidence.quote: (2-RP3) Verify whether the above approach can be transferred to the complex case. Could we then similarly generalise the Haagerup identity?

accepted.question_text: Assuming the copula-realization problem for χ_p or its n-variate version has a positive answer, prove whether the remaining workflow conditions hold: h_b(0)=0 and h_b is a homeomorphism (H), g_b=h_b^{-1} has an absolutely summable real Taylor expansion (RA), f_b is the absolute-coefficient series of g_b (ABS), and f_b(r)=1 for some 0<r<1 (PI(1)); if they hold, compute or numerically approximate the resulting upper bound for the real Grothendieck constant K_G^R, using high-performance computation or computer algebra if needed.

evidence.quote: (H) Assume that hb(0) = 0 and that hb : Dd −→ Dd is a homeomorphism. (RA) Assume that gb := h− 1 b : Dd −→ Dd can be represented as gb(z) = ∑∞ n=1 βn zn for all z ∈ Dd, where βn ∈ R (!) for all n ∈ N and β ≡ (βn)n∈ N ∈ l1; i.e., ∥β∥1 ≡ ∑∞ n=1 |βn|< ∞. (ABS) Put fb(z) := ∑∞ n=1 |βn|zn (z ∈ Dd). (PI(1)) Assume that fb(r) = 1 for some 0 < r < 1.

(2-RP4) If (2-RP1), respectively (2-RP2) holds, prove whether the remaining conditions (H), (RA), (ABS) and (PI1) of the workflow hold. If this were the case calculate (respectively approximate numerically) the related upper bound of K R G. Include high-performance computers and computer algebra systems if necessary.

accepted.question_text: Develop mathematical objects that play the role of “non-commutative copulas” and “non-commutative distribution functions” for modeling non-commutative dependence in quantum theory, in a setting where entanglement, Bell-type phenomena, and Tsirelson-type bounds are linked to the real Grothendieck constant.

evidence.quote: Even a mathematical modelling of non-commutative dependence in quantum theory and its applications to quantum information and quantum computation is strongly linked with the existence of the real Grothendieck constant K R G.
Keeping a non-commutative version of Grothendieck’s inequality at the back of our mind (cf. [33, 38, 39]) these facts might lead to problems of the following type:
(3-RP1) Look for objects like “non-commutative copulas”, leading to a search for “non- commutative distribution functions”.

accepted.question_text: Create a multivariate spectral theory for tuples of non-commuting normal operators and use it to introduce non-commutative tail-dependence measures in non-commutative C*-algebras and operator spaces.
accepted.context_brief: Non-commuting spectral and tail dependence theory

evidence.quote: (3-RP2) Create a “multivariate” spectral theory of non-commuting normal operator tuples and introduce non-commutative tail dependency measures in non-commutative C ∗-algebras and operator spaces.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether the Gaussian structure in Grothendieck’s inequality over both R and C can be replaced by tail-dependent distribution functions, such as generalized extreme value distributions, or by infinitely divisible probability distributions, while preserving the inequality; if such replacement is possible, determine whether it can improve the lower or upper bounds for the Grothendieck constant and whether correlation matrices still suffice in the trace-inequality formulation.

evidence.quote: We finish this research list with a few completely open questions and a conclusion: Can we remove the underlying Gaussian structure in Grothendieck’s inequality (for both fields, R and C) and implement tail dependent distribution functions instead (such as the generalized extreme value (GEV) distribution) and maintain the inequality? If this were the case, could that approach also be used to improve the lower and the upper bound of the Grothendieck constant? What about infinitely divisible probability distributions in general? It is very likely that just the use of correlation matrices in the trace inequality version of GT would then no longer suffice.
